data.title: Peter Schreiber: The occupation of Žilina and its region from the Roman period to the Middle Ages – the site of Divinka
data.excerpt: The summit of Veľký vrch above Divinka is encircled by a simple rampart, with an acropolis on a terrace at its western end and a dark occupation layer containing Late Lusatian, Roman-period and early medieval sherds. Peter Schreiber sums up the surveys of A. Petrovský-Šichman (1952, 1954) and the rescue excavation of J. Moravčík (1972, 1973), and notes that around the middle of the 9th century the central hillfort of the region is assumed to have shifted here from Ostrá skala at Vyšný Kubín.

children.text: The field survey at the site was carried out by A. Petrovský-Šichman (the Regional Museum in Žilina, in 1952 and 1954). The rescue excavation was carried out by J. Moravčík (the Považie Museum in Žilina, in 1972 and 1973). The site of Veľký Vrch - the summit of Veľký vrch has an elongated shape running NW–SE and its highest point lies above the W edge. At the E edge it turns into a platform (possibly artificially levelled). The oldest occupation dates from the Eneolithic (channelled pottery). The whole summit of the hill is encircled by a simple rampart and the acropolis in the western part lies on a terrace. The northern slope of Veľký vrch ends above the Divinka stream in a high rock face. From the edge of the summit of Veľký vrch that projects furthest to the NW, another rampart runs as far as that rock face. In the locality known as Koleso the rampart is missing. From gates II–III to the S–E edge of the platform there is a dark occupation layer on the surface with Late Lusatian sherds and sherds of the Roman period and of the Early Middle Ages. The central part of the hillfort summit between gates II and III and the acropolis was probably not permanently occupied. Across the whole acropolis there is a dark occupation layer with sherds of the Roman period (Petrovský-Šichman 1957, p. 88). The rampart defences (spot height 531 m) probably date from the Hallstatt period; in the Roman period they were apparently rebuilt and extended. On the acropolis there are stone footings of log buildings. Finds: vessels, sherds, nails, spindle whorls, awls, knives, a small whetstone, a buckle, a spur and a bezelled finger ring, dated to the mid-9th – early 10th century (Pramene II 1992, p. 187). To protect the approach to the summit of the hill, a small rampart fortification, Hradisko na Kolárovej, was apparently built in the Roman period. There are also several mound-like features immediately beside the Hradisko enclosure. Pottery from the end of the hillfort period was recorded on the summit of the hillfort at Kolárová (Petrovský-Šichman 1964, p. 71). Before the early medieval fortified settlement at Divinka came into being, the role of the fortified centre of the NW Slovak region was apparently filled by the fortified settlement of Ostrá skala at Vyšný Kubín. Around the middle of the 9th century the hillfort at Divinka, close to Žilina, came into being, and it is assumed that in this case the central hillfort shifted locally (Moravčík 1978b, 58, 59).

(Note by Orgoň: The following photographs were provided to us by Mgr. Andrea Slaná, archaeologist of the Považie Museum in Žilina. The photographs were taken by Anna Kucharčíková, the photographer of the museum. They are finds from Veľký vrch, recovered during Jozef Moravčík's excavation in the 1970s.)

Within north-western Slovakia, the greatest number of burial mounds was in the Žilina Basin and also on the geographical boundary between Žilina and Trenčín. South of Beluša, mound burial is only exceptional. The groups of mounds of the northern Váh region and of the Žilina–Čadca area lie close to one another. These groups therefore appear as one more extensive conglomerate of sites. The hint of a connection between them disappears if the barrow cemeteries of Jasenica, Rašov, Súľov and Podhorie, whose authenticity can be questioned, are separated out of their complex (Hanuliak 2001, 1–2, p. 281). These barrow cemeteries lie on the line linking the two groups mentioned.
(Note by Orgoň: These unique photographs were provided to us by Mr Jozef Jaroš, a resident of the village of Divinka, who collected them in the past)

children.text:
In general, on the basis of the objects of the grave inventory (which have a narrow frequency of occurrence and low chronological sensitivity), we date the sites with the mound burial rite so that their main concentration fills the span from the second half of the 8th century to the first half of the 9th century. According to the most recent view, it would perhaps be possible to link the mound burial custom with a colonising stream of communities penetrating into the relevant areas through the northern Carpathian passes (Bialeková 1993, p. 44, fig. 2), in contrast to the flat graves in the lowland areas settled by the southern stream (Hanuliak 2001, 1–2, p. 294).  
  In northern Slovakia we do not yet know of a single permanently occupied fortification that would have come into being after the Roman period. The results of the excavations carried out so far do not confirm the existence of fortified settlements in the territory of present-day Slovakia, Moravia, the adjoining areas of Lower Austria and Bohemia in the first half of the 7th century (Hulínek – Čajka 2004-1, p. 80). From the Váh region as far as the Turiec region we know of several fortlets with Great Moravian and late medieval remains (Púchov, Hatné, Udiča-Klape, Divina, Radoľa, Turie, Jasenové near Rajec, Strečno-Bašta, Bystrička, Slovenské Pravno). All these fortlets lie in the Žilina and Turiec area, and the area in which fortlets and burial mounds occur coincides geographically (Petrovský-Šichman 1964, pp. 101–102).  
  Peter Schreiber 2005
